title: Which shape does LeetCode use?
prompt: On LeetCode, what do you actually write?
options: A method inside a `Solution` class — no `main`
A full program with `public static void main`
Just the method body, no class or signature
A separate file for each test case
explanation: LeetCode calls your method for you, so you only fill in the method inside `class Solution`. You write the full `main` scaffold only for standalone programs (this course's 'write a program' exercises).

title: Predict the output: + with strings
prompt: Predict exactly what each line prints.
explanation: `+` is evaluated left to right. `"sum = " + 2` is already a String, so `+ 3` appends "3" → `sum = 23`. Parentheses force the math first → `5`. In the last line `2 + 3` runs before any String appears, so it's `5` and then `" apples"` is appended.

title: Recall: the runnable scaffold
prompt: Fill in the entry-point boilerplate every standalone Java program needs.
explanation: `class Main`, then `public static void main(String[] args)` — the fixed signature the JVM looks for to start the program.

title: Drill: write the scaffold from scratch
prompt: From a blank editor, write a complete runnable program that prints exactly `ready`. No starter — reproduce the whole `class` + `main` scaffold yourself.

solution.explanation: The scaffold is always the same — the only thing that changes between programs is what goes inside main.

hints: Every program is a class wrapped around one entry-point method the JVM knows how to find.
Open with `public class Main {`, then the fixed `public static void main(String[] args) {` line.
Inside main: `System.out.println("ready");` — then close both braces.

title: Recall: the LeetCode solution shape
prompt: Fill in the import and the class wrapper you write for LeetCode-style problems.
explanation: `import java.util.*;` for collections, a class named `Solution`, and a method that `return`s its result — no `main` needed.

title: Drill: write a Solution method from scratch
prompt: From a blank editor, write a `Solution` class with a method `boolean isPositive(int n)` that returns whether `n` is greater than 0. Reproduce the whole class + method shape yourself.

solution.explanation: `class Solution { public <returnType> <name>(<params>) { return ...; } }` — internalize this frame and every problem is just filling the body. A comparison like `n > 0` already is a boolean, so return it directly.

hints: LeetCode shape: a class named `Solution` with the method inside — no `main`.
The signature is `public boolean isPositive(int n)`.
A comparison is already a `boolean` — return it directly instead of using if/else.
